opus-5.5.text:
I think the key change is what the main bottleneck is.

In the first half, roughly from the early days of deep learning up to the first big wave of large language models, the game was about **methods**. Someone proposes a new architecture, a new training algorithm, a new prompting technique, and shows it beats the baseline on a benchmark. Transformers, RLHF, chain-of-thought, ReAct: they all fit that pattern. Benchmarks were mostly fixed, and the creative work was in climbing them. That worked really well. Most of the papers we remember are method papers, not benchmark papers.

What changed is that we now have something like a **general recipe**: large-scale pretraining, plus reasoning, plus reinforcement learning, operating in language and acting through tools. The surprising thing is how well this recipe generalizes. Once you have it, a new benchmark tends to get saturated very quickly, sometimes within months, often without any special method designed for it. So if your contribution is "here's a clever trick that adds a few points on this benchmark," that matters a lot less, because the next general model may just get there anyway.

So in the second half, I think the important question becomes: **what should we evaluate, and what problems are actually worth solving?** It moves from "can we solve this task" to "are we defining the right tasks." And there's a real gap. These models can win at competition math or programming contests, yet the economic and real-world impact is still much smaller than you'd expect from those scores. That tells me our evaluation setups are disconnected from reality in important ways.

For example, most benchmarks assume the task runs autonomously: the agent gets an input and produces an output, with no human in the loop. Real work is interactive. You talk to a user, clarify, adjust. Benchmarks also assume tasks are i.i.d.: you solve each one independently and then forget it. But a real software engineer working in the same codebase for months gets better because they accumulate context and memory. Our current setup doesn't reward that at all.

So for language agents specifically, the second half means thinking like a product person, or a researcher who designs environments. You build evaluations and environments closer to real utility, with real users, long horizons, and real feedback, and then use the general recipe, or break it, to make progress there. The people who matter most may not be the ones with the cleverest method. They may be the ones who define the right problem.

r001.rationale: The response says research now has a “general recipe” and that it generalizes well across benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It describes the shift from proposing methods to asking what to evaluate and which problems are worth solving with the general recipe.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I frame it is that the first half of AI was really about training methods and models, and the second half is about defining problems — defining the right evaluation.

For a long time, the bottleneck was: can we make the model do this at all? So the field rewarded new architectures, new training tricks, new ways to do reasoning. Chain of thought, ReAct, tree search over language — those were all about unlocking capabilities that models didn't have. And the benchmark side was relatively easy, because almost any reasonable benchmark would show a huge gap, and the interesting work was closing the gap.

What changed is that we now have a recipe that generalizes. You take a strong pretrained model, you give it language as the interface for both reasoning and acting, and you run reinforcement learning on top of that with verifiable rewards or environment feedback. That combination — language as the prior, plus RL — turns out to work across a surprising range of domains. Math, code, web browsing, software engineering. Once you have a recipe like that, the question is no longer "how do we build the agent." The question becomes "what should the agent be doing, and how do we know it's actually useful."

And that's where I think the field has been lazy. We keep making benchmarks that are harder versions of the same thing — more questions, more digits, more steps — and we measure the model once, in isolation, on independent and identically distributed problems. But that isn't how anything in the real world works. A real assistant has to deal with the same user over time, with ambiguity, with feedback, with tasks where the interaction itself is the hard part. Our evaluation setups don't capture that, so models can saturate every benchmark we have and still not be particularly transformative economically.

So when I say second half, I mean the leverage has shifted. In the first half, if you came up with a better method, you could advance the whole field. In the second half, if you come up with a better problem — a better environment, a better way of measuring real utility — that's what actually moves things. The methods will follow, because the recipe is general enough now. The scarce thing is the taste to define what matters.

It's a little uncomfortable for people like me who came from the methods side. Building a new benchmark used to feel less prestigious than building a new algorithm. I think that has to flip. The people who figure out how to turn messy real-world tasks into environments that models can learn in — that's going to be the core research of the next few years.

r001.rationale: It says the field now has “a recipe that generalizes” and describes language-based reasoning and acting combined with reinforcement learning working across multiple domains.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the first half’s focus on better methods with the second half’s focus on defining the right problems, environments, and measures of utility.

astra-6.text:
I think the shift is from asking, “Can we make a language model act as an agent?” to asking, “Can that agent reliably do something useful?”

In the first half, a lot of the work was about establishing the basic possibility. A model can reason, take an action, observe the result, and then decide what to do next. Once you connect those steps, it can interact with an environment instead of just producing an answer. Even a relatively simple demonstration is exciting because it shows a new capability.

But demonstrating that an agent can complete a task once is very different from having a system that people can depend on. In the second half, the questions become more concrete: Which tasks are actually valuable? How do we measure success? Can the agent recover when something goes wrong? How much time, cost, and human supervision does it require?

That also changes where the research difficulty lies. It’s not only about designing a better reasoning prompt or agent framework. It’s about the whole system—the model, the tools, the environment, and the way we train and evaluate it. A stronger model helps, but we still need to understand how to turn its capabilities into reliable performance over many steps.

So I don’t mean that the first set of problems is solved. I mean that the standard for progress is changing. Showing that an agent can act is the starting point; showing that it can consistently accomplish something worthwhile is the next challenge.

r001.rationale: The response describes basic agent capability as demonstrated, but says the foundational problems are not solved and does not state that research has reached a broadly generalizable method.

r002.rationale: It raises which tasks are valuable as a second-half question, but does not characterize the shift as moving from method development to choosing problems using an available general method; it continues to emphasize building and evaluating the whole system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first half was largely about showing that language models could act as agents at all. Could a model reason through a problem, use a tool, observe the result, and decide what to do next? Language gives us a very flexible interface for connecting those pieces, and getting that loop to work was an important step.

The second half asks a harder question: can that agent reliably accomplish something useful? A successful demonstration is different from a system you can trust with a task that takes hours, involves ambiguous instructions, and requires recovering from mistakes.

That changes where we put our effort. We have to think about the environment, the tools, how to measure success, and how the agent learns from its interactions. Better reasoning still matters, but so does knowing when to check your work or ask the user a question.

So I see the transition as moving from establishing the possibility of language agents to making them dependable in practice. The basic interaction loop is there. Now we have to make it work consistently on problems people actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response says the basic interaction loop works and describes a move toward dependable agents, but it does not state that research has reached a broadly generalizable method.

r002.rationale: The response frames the shift as making agents dependable in practice. It does not identify the central challenge as choosing which problems to solve using an available general method.
